note: Authored demonstration pairs. They are not corpus text and not verified natural ASL.

groups.title: Errors an overlap score misses
groups.blurb: Each gloss differs from a correct reference by one planted error. Sign F1 against that reference stays high.

examples.title: A number changed
examples.look: Same signs, different count. Sign F1 ignores numerals, so it scores this 1.00.

examples.title: Two numbers swapped
examples.english: John saw two birds and three dogs.
examples.gloss: fs-JOHN SEE THREE BIRD TWO DOG
examples.reference: fs-JOHN SEE TWO BIRD THREE DOG
examples.look: Every sign of the reference is present. Only attaching each number to its noun shows the error.

examples.title: Negation dropped
examples.look: No NOT sign, and the head-shake is annotated as absent, so the negation is MISSING.

examples.title: Negation added
examples.look: One extra sign reverses the meaning.

examples.title: Who did it reversed
examples.look: A low-confidence alarm: ASL word order is weak evidence of who did what.

examples.title: A number dropped
examples.english: The teacher helped three students yesterday.
examples.look: The count is stated in English and has no trace in the gloss.

examples.title: Wrong person
examples.look: SISTER is not expressed by any sign.

examples.title: Wrong action
examples.look: The only predicate in the gloss is a different verb.

groups.title: Faithful glosses
groups.blurb: No alarm is raised. A MATCH covers only that fact; it does not say the gloss is good ASL.

examples.title: Plain sentence with a count
examples.look: Negation stays UNKNOWN: with no head-shake labels, a missing NOT proves nothing.

examples.title: Different but equivalent signs
examples.look: The built-in synonym list connects kids to CHILDREN and watch to LOOK.

examples.title: Negation by head-shake only
examples.look: Same gloss as the dropped-negation example. The annotated head-shake carries the negation.

groups.title: Honest UNKNOWN
groups.blurb: When the evidence cannot settle a fact, the checker says so instead of guessing.

examples.title: No head-shake labels supplied
examples.look: Third time for this gloss. Without labels, negation may be on the face, so it is UNKNOWN. Switch the head-shake control to see it change.

examples.title: Topic marker
examples.look: A topic marker can front the object, so word order is no longer role evidence.

examples.title: Classifier predicate
examples.english: The car drove up the hill.
examples.look: The classifier may express both the car and the driving. Neither is flagged.

examples.title: Negative-meaning sign
examples.look: HATE may carry "don't like". The checker abstains on action and negation.

groups.title: Known weak spots
groups.blurb: Where the current rule checker is wrong or silent. These drive the next round of work.

examples.title: False alarm: unlisted synonyms
examples.look: A faithful gloss, flagged with high confidence. The word-to-sign lexicon does not know these synonyms.

examples.title: Missed error: currency
examples.look: The amount changed from 5 to 15. The English reader does not attach "$5", so numbers stay UNKNOWN.
